subtype: Approach: choosing a hobby by what he enjoys not what is popular [Thinking]
passage: Sunday night. My friend Yogesh asked which hobby I am picking and I said cricket, because everyone does. Then on the roof this evening I asked myself: what do I do when nobody is watching? I watch the koel in the neem tree. I count the sparrows at the water bowl. Once I spent an hour on a mynah with a torn feather. Cricket I like when others cheer. So maybe my hobby should be the one I would do alone. Bird watching. Yogesh said "Boring!" and laughed, but not meanly. I will borrow Papa's old binoculars and start a notebook. Maybe Yogesh will come one morning. Harish

qa.q: What does Harish plan to borrow from Papa?
qa.a: Harish plans to borrow Papa's old binoculars.

qa.q: What question did Harish ask on the roof, and what feeling did the answer bring?
qa.a: "What do I do when nobody is watching?" The answer brought clarity and a bit of excitement about bird watching. 🙂

qa.q: How could Harish stay close to friends who love cricket?
qa.a: Invite Yogesh on a morning bird walk and still join a cricket game now and then, because a hobby of one's own need not cost friendships.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel about Harish's choice?
qa.a: Surprised, since Yogesh called it boring, but not unkind, since Yogesh laughed gently and may turn curious later.

grounding: Harish asks what feels enjoyable when nobody watches and picks bird watching over cricket, choosing a hobby of Harish's own.

subtype: Approach: choosing a hobby by what he enjoys not what is popular [Thinking]
passage: Every evening the boys of Mridul's village played cricket on the dry field behind the school, and Neelam kept telling him he'd make a good bowler if he tried. Mridul tried. He bowled, fetched balls from the thorn bushes, and mostly watched the sky. One Sunday he sat alone on the canal bank with his grandfather's old binoculars and saw a kingfisher dive twice. He didn't notice two hours pass. Walking home he asked himself, what would I do if nobody was watching and nobody was cheering? Not cricket. The kingfisher. The next evening he told Neelam, "I'm going to the canal instead. I'll still come on Sundays if you're short." Neelam called him "bird uncle". Mridul took it as a compliment, and started a notebook for his sightings.

qa.q: What bird did Mridul see dive twice?
qa.a: He saw a kingfisher dive twice.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling on the canal bank that he didn't feel on the cricket field?
qa.a: He felt absorbed and happy, so content that two hours passed unnoticed, while at cricket he was mostly bored and watching the sky.

qa.q: What could help Mridul keep his new hobby going?
qa.a: Keeping the sightings notebook and a regular time at the canal, so the hobby has a place in his week, while still joining cricket on Sundays to stay close to friends.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel about Mridul choosing the canal?
qa.a: Neelam may be disappointed at losing a possible bowler and teases him, but Mridul's offer to come on Sundays keeps things friendly.

grounding: Shows a boy asking himself what he enjoys with no one watching, and choosing bird watching over the cricket his friends prefer.

subtype: Approach: choosing a hobby by what he enjoys not what is popular [Thinking]
passage: That summer term, nearly every child in Kofi's class in Leeds joined the junior cricket club, and Beatriz said he should too, because she was. Kofi went to two sessions. He was fine at it. But on Saturday morning he found himself lying on his stomach by the pond in the park, watching a heron stand still for twenty minutes. He asked himself, if nobody saw me do either, which one would I still want? He didn't have to think for long. On Monday he told Beatriz he wasn't joining. "But everyone's going," she said. "I know. It's just not mine." His aunt lent him a bird book, and he started a list on the fridge: heron, moorhen, blue tit. He still watched Beatriz's first match from the boundary, and spotted a wagtail during the second over.

qa.q: What did Kofi watch by the pond on Saturday morning?
qa.a: He watched a heron stand still for twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Kofi say the cricket club was "just not mine"?
qa.a: He felt calm and happy watching the heron, and wanted a hobby he would enjoy even with nobody watching, not just the one everyone else joined.

qa.q: What else could Kofi do if he started to feel left out of the cricket crowd?
qa.a: He could keep turning up to watch matches, as he did, or invite Beatriz on a bird walk, so he keeps his own hobby without losing his friends.

qa.q: How might Beatriz feel when Kofi still comes to watch her first match?
qa.a: She may feel supported and less let down, since he chose a different hobby without dropping her.

grounding: Shows a boy choosing bird watching over the cricket his friends prefer because he enjoys it even when nobody is watching.
